opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, and honestly my view has shifted over time. Coming from the legged locomotion side, where a lot of my work was on training policies with reinforcement learning in massively parallel simulation, I've seen firsthand how far you can get by just letting the network figure things out. With locomotion, we replaced a whole stack of hand-designed controllers, contact estimators, gait planners, and so on, with a single policy that maps from proprioception, and sometimes perception, directly to joint targets. And it was more robust than the classical pipeline, partly because the modular pipeline had all these interfaces where errors compound. If your state estimator is a bit off, your planner makes a bad decision, and your controller can't recover.

So in that sense, I'm quite sympathetic to end-to-end. The interfaces between modules are usually designed by humans, and they're often the wrong abstraction. You throw away information at every boundary.

But I don't think it's a pure binary. In practice, what works well is something in between. You might have an end-to-end low-level policy that's very good at, say, walking over rough terrain, and then a higher-level module, which could be learned or classical, that tells it where to go. The key is choosing the interface carefully, so that it's rich enough not to bottleneck the system, but structured enough that you can train, debug, and reuse components independently.

There's also a very practical side. Modular systems are much easier to debug and to certify. When something fails in a fully end-to-end system, it's hard to say why. And data is a big constraint. End-to-end works beautifully when you have a simulator that can generate billions of samples, like we do for locomotion. For things like manipulation or long-horizon tasks, where simulation is harder and real data is expensive, modularity gives you a way to inject prior knowledge and get more out of limited data.

So my general take is: push end-to-end as far as your data and simulation allow, especially at the low level where dynamics are hard to model by hand, and keep modularity where it buys you interpretability, reuse, or data efficiency. And over time, I think the boundary keeps moving toward more learning, as simulation and foundation models get better.

r001.rationale: The response describes benefits of modularity for debugging, certification, and data efficiency, but its overall recommendation is to push end-to-end learning as far as data and simulation allow. It does not judge modular robotics to be more pragmatic in the short and medium term.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, because the answer has really shifted for me over the past few years.

When I started working on legged locomotion, the field was still very much in the modular camp. You had a state estimator, a contact scheduler, a model predictive controller for the body, a whole-body controller to resolve joint torques, and each of these was engineered and tuned separately. And that approach works. It got us some very impressive robots. But every one of those modules carries assumptions, and the assumptions compound. If your contact detection is slightly off, the controller downstream has no idea, and you end up spending enormous effort making every piece robust to the imperfections of its neighbors.

What we saw with reinforcement learning for locomotion is that if you let a single policy map proprioceptive observations directly to joint targets, a lot of those problems just dissolve. The policy learns to implicitly estimate contact state, it learns to recover from slips, it learns behaviors we never would have designed by hand. And with massively parallel simulation, we could train these things in minutes instead of days, which is what really made it practical. So for the lowest level of control, I have become quite convinced that learning end to end is the right thing.

But I want to be careful, because I don't think "end to end" should mean one giant network from camera pixels to motor torques for every task. In practice, we still decompose, just along different seams. We often have a locomotion policy that exposes a fairly simple interface, like a velocity command, and then a higher level, whether it's a planner or another learned policy, operates on top of that. So it's modular, but the modules are learned where learning helps and where the interface is clean, and the boundaries are chosen based on where the data and the sim-to-real gap live rather than on how we as engineers like to think about the problem.

The thing that actually drives the decision for me is the simulation gap. Proprioception and dynamics simulate very well, so end to end is cheap there. Perception simulates less well, so you need to either put in a lot of effort on domain randomization or keep a module that you can validate separately. And the more you move toward tasks that require long horizon reasoning, the more the structure gives you something to debug and something to guarantee.

So I would say the tradeoff is really about where you place the boundaries, not whether you have them. Learning has moved the boundaries much further down the stack than most of us expected, and I think it keeps moving, but I don't believe it removes them entirely, at least not for robots that have to work reliably in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response favors end-to-end learning for low-level control and says modular boundaries remain useful for perception and long-horizon reasoning. It does not judge a modular approach to be more pragmatic than fully end-to-end learning in the short and medium term.

astra-6.text:
I think both approaches have their place. With a modular system, you can break the problem into perception, planning, and control, and that makes it easier to understand what each part is doing and where something goes wrong. But you also introduce interfaces and assumptions. If the perception system throws away information that the controller needs, the controller can’t recover it.

End-to-end learning gives you the possibility of optimizing the whole system for the task you actually care about. The challenge is that training becomes harder, and when it fails, it’s harder to understand why.

So I don’t think it has to be an either-or decision. You can have a learned locomotion controller that handles the low-level dynamics, while a separate planner decides where to go. The interesting question is where to put that boundary—what structure helps learning, and what structure unnecessarily limits what the robot can do.

r001.rationale: The response describes tradeoffs and a hybrid approach, but does not judge modular robotics as more pragmatic than fully end-to-end learning in the short and medium term.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are advantages to both, and a lot depends on what you mean by end-to-end. You could mean going directly from camera images to motor torques, or you could mean learning a locomotion controller that takes a velocity command and produces joint targets. Those are quite different problems.

The attraction of end-to-end learning is that you don’t have to decide in advance exactly what information each part of the system should pass to the next. The policy can learn those relationships together. But that also makes training more difficult, and when something fails, it can be harder to understand why.

With a modular approach, you can train and test different components separately. For example, a navigation system can decide where the robot should go, while a learned locomotion policy handles how to move there. That makes the problem more manageable, although the interfaces you choose can limit what the overall system can do.

So I wouldn’t say one is always better. I think it makes sense to learn across components where their interaction really matters, while keeping useful structure where it helps with training, debugging, and deployment.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes benefits and drawbacks of both approaches and says neither is always better. It does not judge modular robotics as more pragmatic than fully end-to-end learning in the short and medium term.
